title: Logistic Regression Quiz
description: Test your understanding of logistic regression

questions.text: Despite its name, logistic regression is used for which type of task?
questions.explanation: Despite having 'regression' in its name, logistic regression is a classification algorithm used for binary classification problems (predicting one of two possible outcomes). It uses the sigmoid function to output probabilities between 0 and 1, which are then converted to class predictions.

questions.text: What is the output range of the sigmoid function σ(z) = 1 / (1 + e⁻ᶻ)?
questions.explanation: The sigmoid function always outputs values between 0 and 1, making it perfect for representing probabilities. As z approaches infinity, σ(z) approaches 1, and as z approaches negative infinity, σ(z) approaches 0. At z=0, σ(z)=0.5.

questions.text: What loss function is used to train logistic regression?
questions.explanation: Logistic regression uses binary cross-entropy loss (also called log loss), defined as: Loss = -(1/m) Σ[yᵢ·log(pᵢ) + (1-yᵢ)·log(1-pᵢ)]. This loss function heavily penalizes confident wrong predictions and is specifically designed for binary classification problems.

questions.text: What is the decision boundary in logistic regression?
options: A curved line that separates the classes
The point where the sigmoid function equals 1
The maximum value of the loss function
questions.explanation: The decision boundary is where the model switches from predicting class 0 to class 1, which occurs at P(y=1|x) = 0.5. For 2D data, this creates a straight line (linear boundary). Points on one side are classified as class 0, and points on the other side as class 1. This is a key limitation - logistic regression can only create linear decision boundaries.

questions.text: In a confusion matrix, what does a False Positive (FP) represent?
options: Incorrectly predicted class 1 when actual was class 0
Incorrectly predicted class 0 when actual was class 1
questions.explanation: A False Positive (FP), also called a Type I error, occurs when the model incorrectly predicts class 1 when the actual class is 0. For example, in spam detection, this would be classifying a legitimate email as spam. False positives affect precision: Precision = TP / (TP + FP).

questions.text: Which metric should you prioritize when false negatives are very costly (e.g., missing a disease diagnosis)?
questions.explanation: Recall (also called sensitivity) measures how many actual positives were correctly identified: Recall = TP / (TP + FN). When false negatives are costly (like missing a disease), you want high recall to ensure you don't miss positive cases, even if it means accepting more false positives.

questions.text: What happens when you increase the classification threshold from 0.5 to 0.8?
questions.explanation: Increasing the threshold means you only predict class 1 when very confident (P ≥ 0.8). This makes you more selective, leading to higher precision (fewer false positives) but lower recall (more false negatives, as you miss borderline cases). This is the precision-recall tradeoff.

questions.text: True or False: Logistic regression can naturally handle non-linear decision boundaries without feature engineering.
questions.explanation: False. Logistic regression creates linear decision boundaries (straight lines/planes/hyperplanes). To handle non-linear patterns, you need to engineer features (like polynomial features or interactions) or use a different algorithm. This is a key limitation of logistic regression compared to algorithms like decision trees or neural networks.
